title: Visitors - modern classic - review with photos
transcript: welcome to theater reviews with Paul seven I'm here at the Watermill in Newbury to see visitors the Arts Council has cut its annual funding to the watermelon Newbury which will be a tragedy for UK theater if it means they are no longer able to produce shows like and Bleak expectations soon to open in the West End or their current production of visitors visitors was written by Barney Norris about 10 years ago and has been revived with Mr Norris himself now directing it's a sad but ultimately uplifting play about the long lasting relationship of an elderly couple one of whom is succumbing to dementia contrasted with the Restless insecurity of newer Generations there's poignancy and gentle humor as well as a deep understanding of what makes the characters tick and it's beautifully written both in its construction and in its language keep watching and I'll tell you more about this little gem after my recent visit to a little life where I was bombarded with blood videos screens and violence it was something of a relief to be witnessing a play that relies purely on actors and words the water mill has a small stage and the designers good teeth use it well to create a farmhouse sitting room and to the sides a suggestion of the golden wheat fields that were the business of the farm now ready to harvest the occupants are Edie and Arthur well into their 70s in many ways the play is a eulogy to a rural way of life that has been lost in the rootless consumer-driven modern world they met as very young people and have adapted to each other in the same way as they've lived their lives generally a kind of made to amend they may not have had the family or the holidays they would have liked but they have happy memories they've come to rely on one another and take strength from their shared experience they talk in the relaxed way people do who know and love each other well Edie talks mainly but now as Edie puts it her dementia has created a dam that holds back what she wants to think and say the farm has been in Arthur's Family for three generations but the continuity it and they represent is under threat our son Steve isn't interested in taking over the farm and he's pursued a career in Insurance a young carer Kate has been drafted in to help them in their old age but she is neither skilled nor certain to stay the attitude of the newer generations contrasts with the stoicism and acceptance of the older one and I should say Edie and Arthur now represent a generation even older than when this play was written and nearer to disappearing because ten years on people in their 70s are now usually not like them they're the first Baby Boomers and influenced by the post-world War II permissiveness like Steve who is dissatisfied with his life and whose marriage is on the rocks or the millennial Kate who is drifting aimlessly as Edie says to her you're unsure because you could be anyone really and you don't know which life to have but lady May wonder what other life she might have had but she's content with the one she did if Stephen cater visitors to Edie and Arthur Edie in her more Lucid moments regards us all as visitors to the Earth for the duration of our lives and sees that we must make the most of it which he fears Stephen Kate will not as the Play Moves towards the inevitable closing of the door on Edie and Arthur's life together we learn more about all four characters Edie is revealed to be well written quite a philosopher and in her use of language almost a poet her brain may now be letting her down in her interactions with others but she sees the patterns of sunlight across the room and the wheat Fields changing but eternal tessabelle Briggs his Ed seamlessly segues between warm awareness and drowning in dementia but always retaining the connecting thread as a portrait of dementia it is very moving Arthur is quiet and like many men of that generation not given to showing his emotions which makes the moment all the more poignant when contemplating the prospect of Edie going into a home he breaks down in tears Christopher Ravenscroft gives an extraordinary performance as a shy gentleman whose eyes twinkle with contentment and who is horrified when his lack of social skills causes him to say the wrong thing it's a portrayal so authentic you feel you know him Patrick Toomey plays the middle aged but yet to grow up son and as we find out more about him his initial crassness gives way to a sense that despite his different Life Choices he's quite like his father in his inarticulacy and social blunders Natalie Barkley plays Kate the slightly on edge young woman with blue hair who finds some purpose in her life by caring for his parents despite how I've described the play visitors is not without hope yes life is temporary and usually ends badly but Barney Norris has a message about the value of the kind of Life dominated by things that can't be accounted for by economists and marketeers things like love and self-fulfillment and this contented Rural Life is worth celebrating before people like Edie and Arthur end their visit to our world and it disappears forever I hope you found this review useful and if you did please like comment and subscribe so you'll be the first to know about my future reviews why not visit my website theater.reviews and you can follow me on Twitter Mastodon Instagram and Facebook thank you for watching
